In childhood, this very same voice was a source of endless fascination and obsessive pursuit. I recall how I used to roam frantically through the woods and across open fields, peering eagerly into dense bushes and straining my eyes against the canopy, desperate to catch even a momentary glimpse of the elusive singer. Yet, no matter how far I ran or how carefully I searched, the bird remained unseen. It was a perpetual mystery, a creature that existed only as a sound, always just beyond the horizon of my vision.

The auditory experience acts as a miraculous bridge across time, instantly resurrecting the lost wonder, innocence, and imaginative power of my childhood. The age-old call dissolves the cynicism of adulthood, allowing me to feel once more the thrilling, romantic mystery of a world unfathomed.

In this moment of quiet listening, a profound shift occurs in my perception. The song does not merely evoke nostalgia; it actively alters the reality around me. The rigid, material world of solid trees, heavy earth, and mundane routines begins to soften and yield. Under the spell of the cuckoo's elusive call, the physical landscape transfigures into an enchanted, ethereal realm—an "unreal, fairy place" where memory and reality blur. The earth is no longer just a physical space to inhabit, but a sublime sanctuary fit for visionary dreams, all conjured by the invisible voice of a timeless bird.

For centuries, this elusive creature has captured the human imagination. Renowned for its remarkable migratory journeys, the cuckoo travels thousands of miles across oceans and continents to find its seasonal sanctuary. To hear its distinctive two-note song is to witness nature’s internal clock ticking forward, ushering in **new** growth, warmer winds, and the vibrant rebirth of the natural world.

  And I a boy again.

  And let thy music roll,

Here is the poem in full:

***

### **To the Cuckoo**
*By William Wordsworth*

O blithe New-comer! I have heard,  
I hear thee and rejoice.  
O Cuckoo! shall I call thee Bird,  
Or but a wandering Voice?  

While I am lying on the grass  
Thy twofold shout I hear;  
From hill to hill it seems to pass,  
At once far off, and near.  

Though babbling only to the Vale,  
Of sunshine and of flowers,  
Thou bringest unto me a tale  
Of visionary hours.  

Thrice welcome, darling of the Spring!  
Even yet thou art to me  
No bird, but an invisible thing,  
A voice, a mystery;  

The same whom in my schoolboy days  
I listened to; that Cry  
Which made me look a thousand ways  
In bush, and tree, and sky.  

To seek thee did I often rove  
Through woods and on the green;  
And thou wert still a hope, a love;  
Still longed for, never seen.  

And I can listen to thee yet;  
Can lie upon the plain  
And listen, till I do beget  
That golden time again.  

O blessed Bird! the earth we pace  
Again appears to be  
An unsubstantial, faery place;  
That is a fit home for Thee!

***

### Notable Mention:
If you are interested in a similar masterpiece, **Percy Bysshe Shelley’s "To a Skylark"** (1820) touches on the exact same theme. It opens with the famous lines:

> *"Hail to thee, blithe Spirit! / Bird thou never wert..."*

Shelley describes a skylark that flies so high into the bright sun that it becomes completely invisible to the human eye, leaving only its glorious song pouring down from the sky.
